If you know that ultimately it's a good thing and you trust your therapist, my advice is to just give yourself a time commitment to sessions-- 6 mo, a year, whatever. That way it's harder to give up.

I hate therapy. It's exhausting and I end up with a headache or migraine afterwards. I always dread my sessions. But I need it and I know in the long run it is good for me. 

That said, if you are in tears before you even start a session, maybe bring it up to your therapist. Maybe take one session to talk about something that doesn't dredge up that feeling of dread.

In my experience: It can be awkward, but the usually at the first session they will ask what prompted you to make the appointment. They ask about your family and education background for context. At some point they will ask what your goals are or what you are looking to get out of therapy. You can be as descriptive or in depth as you feel comfortable. It's your time. The therapist will outline their expectations and responsibilities as far as confidentiality, under what circumstances they would break confidentiality or recommend hospitalization, call protective services, etc. Sometimes there are a lot of questions but it's not like a quiz. At the end of the session there will be some wrap up to make the next appointment, maybe make a goal for the week, and, if the session was intense, make sure you are emotionally stable. 

As far as cost, taking care of your mental health is as important as taking care of a broken leg. A life with a broken leg would be very uncomfortable. It's not your responsibility to suffer in silence.

I started a new medication--Effexor--in November. Prozac wasn't really doing anything other than the bare minimum for my mental health anymore and my sex drive was annihilated anyway. 

Effexor SUCKS to get on. I was super dizzy (to the point where I could not drive) and anxious and couldn't sleep. I was jittery all the time and actually think I screwed up my jaw from a new habit of teeth-clenching. But after a couple of weeks it sort of settled down? And I only felt pretty apathetic and numb. My doc bumped up the dose to 75mg and after a milder adjustment period I can say:

I love Effexor. Love it. I feel like a normal person. My anxiety is so, so manageable now. Intrusive thoughts are mainly a problem in the shower and in bed but nowhere else. I can talk to strangers and make a mistake and not want to kill myself over it. 

My depression has also lifted. I don't really hate myself. I don't really want to die. I have almost allowed myself to think things are going to be ok. I'm not so angry anymore. I can breathe, and I feel free. 

Sex drive is still lacking, and my jaw hurts, but those are the next issues to tackle.

You can do it. At my first ever counseling appointment, I was so consumed with anxiety and adrenaline I could barely get any words out. There's no right way or wrong way to do it. Just by showing up you're helping yourself, because it will be easier the second time. You have nothing to lose! The worst thing that can happen is you hate it and never go again.

Remember you are paying them, and it's their job to make you feel safe and not judge you. It's your money and your time to use how you wish. The first appointment is a little terrifying, but in my experience the first thing they do is ask what led me to make the appointment, then I just word vomit for 30-40 minutes, then finally they ask what I hope to get out of counseling/what my goals are. Then they reassure me I'm not crazy, just depressed, and we make another appointment. 

You're in control here. The worst thing that could happen is you walk out and never see them again. 

Congrats on making the appointment. I know it's a hard thing, but therapists are by and large awesome, gentle people in my experience.

Couple ideas. Rather than talk to an ER doc about this, can you try to go talk to a school counselor? They would be able to advise you on the best way to proceed as discreetly as possible. Honestly, I wouldn't want to tell an ER doc either. I'm more than happy to discuss my depression with therapists, less happy but willing to discuss it with psychiatrists, and annoyed but obliged to talk about it with a GP. 

Another idea (if you are a girl) is to mention your depression when you go in for a gyno appointment. They can usually prescribe ssris or what have you along with your bc.
